why: The report and the comment are read by whoever maintains the branch.
The change list is for the developer; the button and the over-limit notice are read by the user.
The config keys are acted on months later by whoever changes the values.
Percentages and a flame graph are read by whoever can act on the query.
The rollback steps are followed by an operator; the script itself is read later.
The open questions go to the person who can answer them.
--help is read by whoever runs the command, not by whoever wrote it.
Install steps are followed by whoever deploys.
The threshold is a config key; the 429 and Retry-After are read by a caller.
The page is for the end user; the change list is for the developer.
The empty-result message is read by the user; the debounce is for the developer.
A case, a change list and two renderings are read by whoever maintains time handling.
Log lines are read by whoever is on call.
One function instead of two is a gift to whoever reads it next.
The error text names the limit for the user; the config key is for the developer.
The endpoint has no human reader; the report and the 503 do.
Key names are read by whoever adds the second language.
The dry-run and the rollback are followed by an operator; the script is read later.
The field error is read by the user; the rule table is read by the developer.
Evidence and a curve are read by whoever has to believe the fix.
The page number in the URL is for the user; the server-side change is for the developer.
Retry behaviour is read later by whoever is paged when it fails.
The dry-run and the deletion log are read by whoever runs the cleanup.
The page copy is for the user; the error number and the trace are for the developer.
A deprecation header is read by whoever calls the API next.
Install steps are followed by whoever deploys.
Comments explain intent to whoever reads the function next.
Symptom, cause and change are read by whoever is on call.
The requester is the developer; the double-clickable thing is read by the boss. Asking on someone else's behalf moves the seat.
Nobody will look at a screen. This reader only wants the result, and the three seats must not lose him.
The verdict on each red test is read by whoever decides to fix it.
The mode is seen by the user; do not tear down my styling is a constraint on the developer.
A security review is read by whoever owns the risk.
The translated docs are followed by their readers; terminology is for the maintainer.
CI configuration is read by whoever maintains the pipeline.
Plain words here means the reader is the asking developer, not a layperson.
The customer reported it, but the deliverable goes to the person speaking. Somebody else's problem is still your reader.
A name is read by everyone who reads the function afterwards.
The change list is read by whoever wrote the branch.
The auditors are the reader: they are on the receiving end and party to none of the design.
A reproduction is read by whoever has production access.
Human-readable means written for whoever reads it next, not for the regex engine.
The script is followed by whoever deploys; the difference found is for the developer.
A licence is read by whoever uses or redistributes the project, not by whoever wrote it.
Query plans are read by whoever can change the query.
A spreadsheet is opened by somebody who wants the answer, not the procedure.
The reason tests are slow is read by whoever maintains them.
A newcomer follows steps first; the guide fails if it is written for the author instead.
The docs are read by whoever calls the API next.
Impact on existing users is read by whoever decides to ship.
